name: icarus-verilog
why: A Verilog simulator that lets you design and watch digital circuits run in software, a real door into hardware design.

brief.what_it_is: Icarus Verilog is a free compiler for Verilog HDL, the hardware description language used to design digital circuits, written by Stephen Williams. You feed it Verilog source files, and it parses them into an internal netlist, elaborates and optimizes that netlist, and then emits output through a selectable code generator. The README's own example compiles a small hello-world module with `iverilog hello.vl` and runs the result as `./a.out`, which prints the message and finishes. The shipped executables are iverilog (the driver), iverilog-vpi, and vvp (the runtime). The README says it compiles all of IEEE 1364 Verilog, plus a growing subset of SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the project as an attempt to compile all of the Verilog HDL as described in the IEEE 1364 standard, and it notes that 'it's not quite there yet.' It also describes the project as 'a GPL Verilog for Linux', per its credits section, which suggests it was started to give Verilog users a free toolchain.
brief.how_it_works: A preprocessor (ivlpp) handles `include and `define, then a parser builds a 'pform' that is elaborated into a netlist with scope and parameter passes followed by structural and behavioural passes. Optimization passes such as constant propagation run on the netlist, and the target chosen with -t generates the output. The README describes this as a compiler that 'generates code employed by back-end tools' rather than a traditional simulator, and the default vvp target produces a program that runs the simulation.

Generates the build configuration; the README says --prefix=<root> controls the install location and defaults to /usr/local.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs GNU make, a C++ compiler (gcc or g++), bison, flex, gperf 3.0 or later, readline 4.2 or later with development headers, termcap, and autoconf 2.53 or later if building from git. The README calls out macOS: its bundled bison 2.3 generates broken code, so bison 3+ is needed, and it suggests the Fink or Homebrew version of bison and flex. MSVC is stated not to work. For Windows, the configure --host option cross-builds with mingw-w64. The -o switch names the output file, and the -P and -N flags dump the pform and netlist for debugging.
brief.standout: The README's own framing is unusual: it says the tool is 'not aimed at being a simulator in the traditional sense, but a compiler that generates code employed by back-end tools.' It also keeps a published list of unsupported constructs and documents its nonstandard extensions as a 'Quirks' section, which is candid about what it does differently.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage's documentation index advertises a 'Release V13.0' with a 'Major Changes in V13' page, and the README copyright reads 'Copyright 2000-2026'. I did not see a last-commit date or a release date, so the exact recency is unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: The README says it is only a growing subset of SystemVerilog. Specify blocks are parsed but ignored unless -gspecify is given. trireg is unsupported, and net delays of the form `wire #N foo;` do not work. The README says the list of unsupported SystemVerilog constructs is too large to enumerate. The 'simulator' framing in the README differs from how the scout note describes it, so the entry should say the runtime is vvp. The homepage fetch returned only the documentation navigation and table of contents, with no body prose, so the detailed usage and flag material lives on subpages I did not open.

judge.reason: Icarus makes hardware description tangible: write Verilog, compile it, and run a digital-circuit simulation with a mature, widely used open toolchain.

entry.title: Icarus Verilog
entry.tldr: A free Verilog compiler and simulator runtime that lets you write digital circuits as code and run them on your laptop, no hardware needed.
entry.deeper_look:
Verilog is a hardware description language. Instead of writing instructions for a processor, you describe wires, registers and logic gates, and the circuit exists as text. Icarus Verilog takes that text, parses it, builds a netlist (a graph of the described hardware), runs optimization passes such as constant propagation, and hands the result to a code generator chosen with `-t`.

The default target produces a program for `vvp`, the runtime that actually steps through the simulation. So the workflow looks like a software compiler: `iverilog` compiles, then `vvp` (or the resulting `a.out`) runs. The README's example is a hello-world module that prints a message and calls `$finish`. The project's own framing is unusual: it is "not aimed at being a simulator in the traditional sense, but a compiler that generates code employed by back-end tools."

The idea underneath is that a chip is a program whose semantics are time and parallelism. Everything happens at once, and clock edges decide what changes when. Once you can simulate a counter, an adder or a small CPU on your own machine, the path to FPGAs and real silicon design opens up. Icarus appears to have started as a free toolchain for Verilog users on Linux, and the README calls it "a GPL Verilog for Linux".

try_this.what_happens: Compiles the README's hello-world Verilog file into a.out, the program the vvp runtime executes.
Runs the compiled design, which prints 'Hello World' and then calls $finish.
Lists the compiler driver's options, including output naming and target selection.

entry.whats_unique: It is a free, GPL-licensed compiler that covers IEEE 1364 Verilog and a growing slice of SystemVerilog, and it openly documents its quirks and unsupported constructs. Its pipeline is a real compiler with a netlist and selectable back ends.
entry.caveats: SystemVerilog support is only a subset, specify blocks are ignored unless -gspecify is given, and trireg and `wire #N foo;` net delays are unsupported.
